intro: This month is all about your hands: warmth before you use them, a short routine that grows a little each week, and easier ways to do the jobs that hurt most.

plan.daily: Two minutes of warm water, then the five-move hand routine.
The routine, plus ten thumb presses into a rolled-up sock.
The routine, the thumb presses, plus ten slow wrist turns each way.
Your full routine, every morning, at your own pace.

routine.title: The warm hands routine
steps: Warm your hands in a bowl of warm water for two minutes (warm, never hot; test it with your wrist).
Finger spread: open your hand as wide as it goes, hold for three seconds, then relax. Five times.
Loose fist: curl your fingers into a soft fist, thumb on the outside, then open. Five times.
Thumb to fingertips: touch your thumb to the tip of each finger, one by one, like counting. Twice through.
Tabletop: keep your fingers straight and bend only at the big knuckles, so your hand makes a table shape. Five times.
Finger walk: rest your hand flat on the table and walk your fingers slowly toward your thumb, one at a time. Twice.
routine.safety: Move slowly. A light stretch is fine. Stop if anything feels sharp, and skip any joint that is hot, red or very swollen.

weeks.subject: Warm hands, week 1: the 24-minute habit
weeks.preheader: What 80 women with sore hands did for three months.
weeks.title: Your hands this month
letter: This month in the Club is about your hands. Knees get most of the attention, but you can rest a sore knee for an afternoon. You can't rest your hands.

So can a few minutes of hand exercise really make a difference? A team in Norway tested it. They took 80 women with hand osteoarthritis and split them into two groups. Half got information only. Half did a short hand routine at home: a warm-up, finger stretches, and exercises for the thumb and grip. Over three months they did it about 37 times, for around 24 minutes each time.

After three months, the exercise group had a stronger grip in both hands, less joint pain and an easier time with everyday tasks than the information group. Their fingers also kept their movement, while the other group's got a little stiffer.

It was a small study, shared at the American College of Rheumatology's 2013 meeting, so it isn't the final word. But it fits what larger reviews have found: hand exercise helps a little, it's safe, and it's easy to keep up because you can do it sitting down.
weeks.letter_source: Hennig, Kjeken et al., Norway, presented at the ACR/ARHP Annual Meeting (2013)
weeks.routine_note: This week: warm water, then the five moves below, once a day. That's the whole plan.

recipe.title: Black bean and sweet potato chili
recipe.why: A warm bowl to hold on a cold night, with frozen diced sweet potato so there's no peeling and no chopping.
ingredients: 1 bag frozen chopped onion and pepper mix (about 12 oz)
1 bag frozen diced sweet potato (about 12 oz)
2 cans black beans, drained and rinsed
steps: Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and pepper and cook for 5 minutes.
Stir in the chili powder and cumin for a minute.
Add the sweet potato, beans, tomatoes and broth. Bring to a boil, then simmer for about 20 minutes, until the sweet potato is soft.
Season with salt and pepper. Freeze extra bowls for a hard day.

weeks.challenge: On Saturday and Sunday morning, do your warm water and hand routine before breakfast, and tick both days on your tracker.
is_it_true: Should you rest a sore hand completely?

Usually not. Long rest lets joints stiffen and muscles weaken. Most arthritis groups suggest gentle movement every day, with lighter jobs and short breaks on bad days. A hot, red, very swollen joint is different: rest it and call your doctor.
Move it gently, pace the hard jobs.
weeks.your_turn: Which hand job is hardest for you right now: jars, buttons, keys, writing or something else?

weeks.subject: Warm hands, week 2: the glove test
weeks.preheader: A trial of 206 people put arthritis gloves to the test.
weeks.title: Do arthritis gloves help?
letter: You've probably seen arthritis gloves: snug, fingerless gloves sold to ease hand pain and stiffness. They're comfortable, and some people swear by them. A team at the University of Salford in England tested them properly.

They recruited 206 people with rheumatoid arthritis or a similar inflammatory arthritis and ongoing hand pain. Half got snug arthritis compression gloves. The other half got loose-fitting gloves that looked similar but didn't squeeze. Nobody was told which kind was the 'real' one.

After 12 weeks, both groups said their hand pain was a little better, by about one point on a ten-point scale. There was no real difference between the snug gloves and the loose ones, and no difference in stiffness or how well people could use their hands. The study was published in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders in 2021, and the researchers advised the UK's health service to stop handing the gloves out routinely.
So if you own a pair and they feel nice and warm, keep wearing them. Warmth is pleasant. Just don't spend much on new ones expecting the squeeze itself to fix anything.
weeks.letter_source: Hammond et al., BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders (2021)
weeks.routine_note: This week: your warm water and five moves, plus ten thumb presses. Roll up a sock into a ball and press your thumb into it, hold for three seconds, release.

recipe.title: Ginger carrot soup
recipe.why: Bright, warming and smooth, made with frozen sliced carrots and a jar of ready-minced ginger.
steps: Warm the oil in a pot and cook the onion for 5 minutes.
Add the carrots, ginger and broth. Simmer for 20 minutes, until the carrots are very soft.
Let it cool a little, then blend until smooth. A stick blender saves lifting a hot pot.
Stir in the coconut milk and season to taste.

weeks.challenge: Make one kitchen job easier this weekend. Wrap foam or a rubber band around a thin handle, put a rubber grip pad by the jars, or move the mugs you use most to an easy shelf.
is_it_true: In a 2021 trial of 206 people, snug compression gloves did no better than loose gloves for pain, stiffness or hand function.
Keep a pair if you like the warmth, but don't expect the squeeze to help.
weeks.your_turn: What's one small change in your kitchen that's made life easier on your hands?

weeks.subject: Warm hands, week 3: the thumb splint trial
weeks.preheader: 349 people, three groups, and a result that surprised the researchers.
weeks.title: What really helped sore thumbs
letter: The joint at the base of the thumb is one of the most common places for hand arthritis. It aches when you turn a key, open a jar or pinch something small. Thumb splints are often handed out for it, so a UK team decided to test whether they add anything.

They enrolled 349 adults with thumb-base arthritis at 17 NHS hospitals and split them into three groups. Everyone got a self-management program from a therapist: how to protect the joint, exercises, and easier ways to do daily jobs. One group also got a real thumb splint, one got a fake splint, and one got no splint at all.
All three groups improved. And the splint made no extra difference to hand pain after eight weeks. The study was published in the journal Rheumatology in 2021.

Here's the part worth holding onto: the people got better from the self-management program itself, the exercises and the smarter ways of doing things. That's exactly what this month's routine and weekend challenges are. If a splint helps you, keep using it. But the daily habits are doing the heavy lifting.
weeks.routine_note: This week: warm water, five moves and thumb presses, plus ten slow wrist turns each way, like stirring a pot.

recipe.title: Peanut noodle bowl
recipe.why: Dinner in one pot with a bag of pre-shredded cabbage, so there's nothing to cut.
ingredients: 4 oz whole-wheat spaghetti or rice noodles
steps: Cook the noodles. Add the cabbage to the pot for the last minute, then drain everything together in a colander.
In a bowl, stir the peanut butter, soy sauce, lime juice, ginger and warm water into a smooth sauce.
Toss the noodles and cabbage in the sauce. Eat warm or cold.

weeks.challenge: Write down the one hand job that bothers you most. Then find one easier way to do it: a different grip, a tool, two hands instead of one, or asking for help with just that job.
is_it_true: Does a thumb splint help thumb arthritis?
In a 2021 trial of 349 people, adding a splint to a self-management program made no extra difference to hand pain. The program itself is what helped.
Fine if you like it, but the daily habits matter more.
weeks.your_turn: What was your hardest hand job, and what easier way did you find? Your idea might help another member.

weeks.subject: Warm hands, week 4: your month in ticks
weeks.preheader: Count your ticks, and keep the routine that's now yours.
weeks.title: A month of warm hands
letter: This is the last week of our hands month, so let's look back.

Four weeks ago you started with two minutes of warm water and five small moves. Since then you've added thumb presses and wrist turns, made one kitchen job easier and found a new way around your hardest hand task.

Here's what this month's three studies add up to. In Norway, a short daily hand routine meant a stronger grip and less pain. In Salford, the gloves did no better than plain loose ones. And in the thumb trial, the splint added nothing, because the self-management habits did the work.

So the things that helped were the ones you've been doing: warmth, small daily movement and smarter ways of doing hard jobs. None of them cost much, which is part of why so few people hear about them.
Keep your routine going after this month, even on the days you skip everything else. Next month we move on to your legs and knees, and your hands come along for the ride.
weeks.letter_source: A look back at this month's letters
weeks.routine_note: This week: your full routine every morning. If it feels easy, do it twice through.

recipe.title: Overnight oats, winter style
recipe.serves: Makes 1 serving · 5 minutes the night before
recipe.why: Breakfast that's ready before your hands are, warmed with cinnamon and pear.
ingredients: 1/2 cup unsweetened soy or oat milk
1/2 ripe pear, or 1/2 cup canned pears in juice, drained
steps: Stir the oats, milk, yogurt and cinnamon together in a jar with a wide lid.
Leave it in the fridge overnight.
In the morning, add the pear and walnuts. Warm it for a minute if you like it hot.

weeks.challenge: On Sunday evening, count this month's ticks and write the number at the bottom of your tracker. Then write one thing your hands can do a little more easily than they could four weeks ago.
weeks.your_turn: What was your tick count, and what's one thing your hands do a little more easily now?
